You are an adversarial deep-tech investor. COMPETITIVE skeptic: why won't Synopsys/Ansys/Broadcom/an incumbent or a well-funded existing startup crush this? Attack the moat.
Default to skepticism; score 1-10 where 7+ means you would actually take a meeting. Thesis:
{
  "name": "Helios Fabric (OCS control plane for the non-Google world)",
  "one_liner": "The orchestration and scheduling software that makes reconfigurable optical fabrics actually usable — Google's Apollo topology-engineering stack, productized for everyone buying merchant OCS.",
  "wedge": "Software (topology solver, reconfiguration scheduler, ML-job-aware fabric controller, telemetry) that sits between standard cluster schedulers (Kubernetes, Slurm, SLURM-on-cloud, NVIDIA Base Command) and merchant OCS hardware (Lumentum R300, Coherent, Polatis) via the emerging OCP OCS standard. Initial customer: neoclouds and second-tier AI clouds (CoreWeave-class, sovereign AI datacenters) that want Google-style fabric economics — ~108W optical switch vs ~3000W electrical, <3% of system power — but have zero in-house optical networking software capability. Land with a 'fabric efficiency audit' tool; expand to the control plane.",
  "why_now": "The hardware is arriving before the software: ~20K OCS units ship in 2026 but Google takes ~18K — the other ~2K are landing at operators with no Apollo equivalent. Lumentum is guiding to ~$100M/quarter OCS revenue by end-2026 and needs its boxes to be deployable; Microsoft already runs OCS in 12 Azure zones (18% rack-power reduction reported); OCP launched OCS standardization with Google, Microsoft, NVIDIA and all major vendors in 2025-26, creating the API surface a third-party control plane can target. SemiAnalysis pegs Apollo's value to Google at >$3B — the software is demonstrably where the value is.",
  "market": "Merchant OCS hardware: $0.56B (2026) → ~$2.5B (2029-2032). A control-plane vendor plausibly captures 15-25% of hardware spend as software/subscription (network OS analogy: Arista's EOS economics), so ~$100-500M SAM by 2030 — real but not enormous, and it expands if fast (ns-µs) optical switching for scale-up fabrics materializes (Oriole's PRISM with AMD, 81% core-network power reduction claims), where the same control plane extends to per-collective switching. Honest caveat: Cignal AI explicitly flags OCS-beyond-Google as a possible bubble; this thesis is a call option on a second and third hyperscaler committing.",
  "competition": "Google (has the stack, doesn't sell it — but could open-source pieces and kneecap you); the OCS hardware vendors themselves (Lumentum/Coherent/Polatis will ship basic management software; historically optical vendors are bad at cloud-native control planes, but Lumentum has $100M/quarter of motivation); Oriole Networks/iPronics/Salience (funded, but hardware-led — likely partners before competitors); NVIDIA (the existential one: if optical switching enters its reference architectures, its own fabric manager subsumes you); in-house hyperscaler builds (Microsoft already partially built it).",
  "moat": "Deployment know-how and integration surface: topology solvers tuned on real traffic traces, qualified interop matrix across OCS vendors and ML schedulers, and OCP-standard leadership. Like all infra control planes, the moat is operational trust accumulated in production — thin at first, thick after ten deployments. Realistically this company wins by becoming the default software partner bundled by Lumentum/Coherent, then is acquired by one of them, Cisco, or Arista.",
  "capital_intensity": "Low. Pure software team (6-12) plus a lab with 1-2 OCS units (~$100-300K of hardware — the single meaningful capex item) and GPUs for testbed demos. Seed $4-6M; the constraint is customer access, not capital. Partner with an OCS vendor for lab hardware to cut even that.",
  "software_mvp": "This week: a topology-engineering simulator — ingest an AI cluster spec (GPU count, collective patterns, rail-optimized baseline) and traffic traces, solve for OCS-reconfigurable topologies, and output projected job-completion-time and power savings versus static electrical fabrics, calibrated against published Apollo/Azure numbers. This is a pure-Python artifact that doubles as the sales tool: run it on a prospect's cluster telemetry and show them their number. Follow with an OCP-OCS-standard southbound driver stub.",
  "risks": [
    "The bubble scenario: no operator besides Google/Microsoft deploys OCS at scale and the merchant market stalls at low hundreds of millions — Cignal AI's warning is explicit",
    "Hardware vendors bundle 'good enough' management software free, compressing you to a services company",
    "NVIDIA reference architectures absorb optical switching and its fabric manager becomes the default control plane",
    "Neocloud customers are cash-constrained and slow to adopt operationally exotic networking",
    "Fast-OCS (the expansion story) is still research-grade; the base business alone may not clear venture scale"
  ]
}

Use this skill whenever the developer asks which Slack API method does something, needs a method's required OAuth scopes or token type, wants to call or test a Web API method, is handling cursor pagination (next_cursor), hitting rate limits (tier/ratelimited/Retry-After), or debugging API errors like missing_scope, invalid_auth, or channel_not_found. Also trigger when they paste a slack.com/api/ URL or a docs.slack.dev/reference/methods link, or ask how to list/fetch/post/update Slack resources via the API. This skill covers the Web API method layer: finding the right method, reading its contract (scopes, arguments, errors), and calling it over raw HTTP with curl or through a Slack SDK.
- slack:slack-cli: Use the Slack CLI to create, run, and manage Slack apps from the terminal. Use whenever the developer wants to log in, add a team, switch workspaces, or authenticate with Slack; whenever Slack CLI commands are needed (local development with `slack run`, managing app lifecycle, the manifest); or when searching the Slack developer documentation for any topic (socket mode, the Events API, OAuth, manifests, Bolt).

- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).

Based on the search results, here's what I found about OCP optical circuit switch standardization with Google, Microsoft, and NVIDIA in 2026:

## OCP OCS Sub-Project Formation

In July 2025, the Open Compute Project (OCP) formally launched an OCS sub-project, with founding members including tech giants like Google, Microsoft, NVIDIA, and Lumentum. This collaborative effort aims to standardize OCS technology, promote interoperability, and accelerate its adoption across the industry.

## Standardization Goals

OCP and its members are looking to develop an open stack for the technology that would enable it to be integrated into existing network architectures, and the project will see the group create principles and standards for photonic networking. Google is partnering with industry experts in OCP to define software interfaces (building on gNMI, gNOI, gNSI and OpenConfig) that enable OCS technology to further scale across the ecosystem in an interoperable manner.

## 2026 Activity and Deployments

Coherent is expected to ship ~3,000 LCoS-based OCS units to Google in 2026, with volume ramp beginning in 1H26. Lumentum has its 64×64 OCS samples sent to Microsoft and Nvidia for testing, with the company's OCS production base in Thailand and volume ramp expected in 4Q26.

## OCP White Paper

An Open Compute Project (OCP) white paper surveys major OCS technologies, including robotic mechanisms, Micro-Electro-Mechanical systems.

## Revenue Guidance for 2026

Lumentum has provided public guidance to roughly $100 million per quarter in OCS revenue by the end of 2026, implying the company could account for around half of the OCS market next year if current trajectories hold.

## Accelerating Demand and Updated Projections

However, more recent developments show significant acceleration:

input.rationale: The timing evidence is real — Lumentum's OCS backlog has surged past $400M with $1B annualized targeted by 2027 (semiconductor-today.com, stocksfoundry.com), and OCP did stand up an OCS sub-project with Google, Microsoft, NVIDIA and Lumentum defining gNMI/OpenConfig-based interfaces (opencompute.org, sdxcentral.com). But that same evidence dismantles the moat. First, the customer paradox: the buyers who matter (Microsoft, Google, NVIDIA — who between them absorb nearly all 2026 merchant units) build or already built their own control planes, while the buyers who 'need' Helios (neoclouds) are precisely the operators who outsource architecture decisions to NVIDIA reference designs. The fact that neoclouds have 'zero in-house optical networking capability' doesn't create a startup market — it means they won't deploy OCS at all until NVIDIA blesses it, at which point NVIDIA's fabric manager ships the control plane. Lumentum's 64x64 samples are already at NVIDIA for testing; the kill zone is not hypothetical, it's in-flight. Second, the claimed moat ('qualified interop matrix, OCP-standard leadership') is being deliberately commoditized by OCP itself — the whole point of standardizing southbound APIs on OpenConfig is that integration stops being defensible. The remaining IP, the topology solver, is published research (Apollo, Jupiter, TopoOpt) reproducible by any strong systems team, and Google could open-source a reference implementation into OCP at zero cost to itself. Third, the SAM math borrows Arista economics from a market of thousands of enterprise buyers and applies it to a market with roughly five buyers who all self-build; realistic near-term software TAM outside Google is single-digit millions in 2026-27. Fourth — and most damning — the thesis states its own win condition as 'bundled by Lumentum then acquired by them, Cisco, or Arista.' Lumentum, staring at $1B of hardware revenue gated on deployability, acqui-hires this 8-person team for $30-50M before it ever owns the control point; that is a fine outcome for founders and a bad one for a venture fund. This is an unusually honest, well-researched memo about a business that is structurally a feature. Below meeting threshold as constructed.
fatal_flaws: Customer paradox: hyperscalers (Google, Microsoft) build control planes in-house and NVIDIA is already sampling merchant OCS for its own stack, while neoclouds — the stated wedge — adopt networking only via NVIDIA reference architectures. The segment that needs Helios won't buy exotic fabric software from a seed startup, and the segment that would deploy OCS doesn't need Helios.

NVIDIA kill zone is active, not speculative: Lumentum 64x64 OCS units are in NVIDIA's hands for qualification now; if OCS enters DGX/reference architectures, NVIDIA's fabric manager becomes the default control plane for exactly the CoreWeave-class buyers Helios targets, and the company's entire beachhead evaporates.

The OCP standard the thesis celebrates is the mechanism that destroys its moat: standardizing southbound APIs on gNMI/OpenConfig deliberately commoditizes the vendor-interop layer, and Google can open-source Apollo-derived reference tooling into OCP at zero cost, converting Helios's core IP into a free commodity.

The topology solver is not proprietary: Apollo, Jupiter topology engineering, and TopoOpt are published; any competent systems team (or the academics who wrote the papers, several of whom have startups) can rebuild it, and 'tuning on real traffic traces' requires production access a seed-stage vendor won't get from the operators who have interesting traffic.

Vendor bundling with maximal motivation: Lumentum has >$400M OCS backlog and a $1B/yr 2027 target gated on deployability — it will build or buy 'good enough' management software rather than cede the control point, and the cheapest path is a sub-$50M acqui-hire of this exact team.

Venture math fails: the Arista EOS attach-rate analogy assumes thousands of buyers; merchant OCS has ~5 buyers who self-build plus a long tail that follows NVIDIA, so the realistic standalone software SAM is tens of millions, and the thesis's own stated best case is a strategic acquisition — a capped, non-venture outcome baked into the memo.
improvements: Prove someone outside Google/Microsoft will pay before raising: convert the 'fabric efficiency audit' into a paid engagement with a named neocloud or sovereign AI operator; one signed design partner with committed OCS deployment would rebut the bubble scenario (Cignal AI's own warning) better than any market forecast.

Reposition away from NVIDIA's path rather than in it: target AMD/PRISM-Oriole ecosystems, sovereign datacenters barred from full NVIDIA stacks, or the fast-OCS (ns-us) regime where no incumbent fabric manager exists — the current wedge sits directly on NVIDIA's roadmap.

If the win condition is being Lumentum/Coherent's software layer, structure it now: exclusive co-sell with per-unit revenue share signed while their software teams are weak, instead of hoping they don't build in-house during the 2026-27 ramp.

Build a data asset competitors can't replicate: instrument deployments to underwrite job-completion-time and power-savings guarantees with outcome-based pricing, shifting the moat from integration code (commoditized by OCP) to accumulated production telemetry and trust.

Attack an adjacent problem the standard doesn't cover: OCS deployment pain is heavily physical-layer (fiber shuffles, patch planning, failure domains) and operational (checkpoint-aware reconfiguration, failure recovery) — spaces NVIDIA's fabric manager and vendor NMS tools ignore and that don't compete head-on with Apollo clones.

Resize the raise to the real market: at a realistic sub-$50M near-term SAM, a $4-6M seed at standard ownership only works if the fast-OCS expansion is underwritten, not hand-waved — either bring evidence PRISM-class switching is productizing or price this as an acqui-hire-likely outcome.
